newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: FOCUS-Bank Austria H1 profit up, bullish for year.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Bank Austria H1 profit up, bullish for year.

text.p: Bank Austria, presenting its first fully consolidated earnings since taking over rival Creditanstalt, reported a 25 percent jump in first half operating profit on Monday.
The group's strong first half performance, combined with a bullish full-year forecast, sent Bank Austria and Creditanstalt shares higher in Vienna on brisk turnover.
Bank Austria preferred shares peaked at 441.95 schillings, 3.95 up on the day, before falling back slightly. Creditanstalt preferred advanced 12.35 schillings to a high of 577.55.
Bank Austria, which controls more than 75 percent of Creditanstalt voting stock, said group operating profit jumped to 7.12 billion schillings from 5.67 billion the previous year.
"The great thing for Bank Austria is that it has Creditanstalt," said Gerhard Auer, analyst at ICE Securities.

Creditanstalt had flagged the higher earnings on Friday when it announced a 38 percent surge in its operating result to 4.2 billion schillings ($324 million) thanks to a strong international performance and robust trading profits.

"(An increased dividend) looks to be a possibility for the entire group," Bank Austria board member Karl Samstag told a news conference, raising the prospect of a pay-out above last year's 12 schillings per share.
Samstag added Austria's largest banking group was "more likely than not" to beat its target of a 12 billion schillings operating profit for the full year.

"It looks as though the first half went better than expected but a lot of that is down to trading profits, which could tail off in the second half," cautioned James Alexander, an analyst at Kleinwort Benson in London.
Bank Austria's operating income climbed 13 percent to 21.5 billion schillings, outstripping an eight percent rise in operating expenses to 14.38 billion schillings.
Trading income leapt 76 percent to 2.72 billion schillings.

Auer predicted Bank Austria's strategy of selling off industrial holdings and concentrating on core business would boost future profits. Earnings from investments stood at 1.57 billion schillings in the first six months, a 40 percent rise.
"The reasons people are bullish on German banks -- selling industrial holdings and refocusing -- apply equally to Bank Austria," he said.

Investors would be watching with interest to see what the group did with Creditanstalt's interest in building materials firm Wienerberger and Bank Austria's stake in viscous fibre maker Lenzing, Auer added.
Some analysts expressed slight disappointment at the level of net interest income, which was flat at 11.69 billion schillings.
Commission income rose 10.7 percent to 4.33 billion schillings and personnel expenses increased 7.3 percent to 8.2 billion schillings. ($ = 12.96 Austrian Schillings)
